[Chapter 1](native-book-1-mean-structure.html) built the mean structure. This
chapter asks what happens when the variables sit far from zero relative to their
spread, a common situation (a test score near 500 with a spread of 10, a year near
2000), and shows the change of coordinates the engine uses so that the answer does
not depend on where the data sit. The engine is experimental.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You need** | Chapter 1 (the RAM matrices $A$, $S_{\text{ram}}$, $m$, the implied mean and the expected information) |
| **You get** | why the information matrix goes singular as the means grow, the centered coordinates $\phi$ and the map $\theta = T(\phi + c_0)$, the identity $V = T V_\phi T^\top$, and the exact conditions under which the engine fits shifted data |
| **Time** | about 35 minutes |

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(medfit)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
rd <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)
sci <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = d)

syntax <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
"
base <- mediation_demo[, c("treatment", "mediator1", "outcome")]
# the same data moved far from zero: means 100 to 300 ("mid"), then 1e3 to 1e5 ("big"),
# against standard deviations of 0.5 to 1.3
mid <- base
mid$treatment <- mid$treatment + 100
mid$mediator1 <- mid$mediator1 + 100
mid$outcome <- mid$outcome + 300
big <- base
big$treatment <- big$treatment + 1e3
big$mediator1 <- big$mediator1 + 1e4
big$outcome <- big$outcome + 1e5
rbind(mean_mid = colMeans(mid), mean_big = colMeans(big), sd = apply(base, 2, sd)) |> rd(2)
```

Adding a constant to a variable changes its mean and nothing else about it: the
variances, covariances and every regression path are exactly what they were. A good
estimator should return the same paths, variances and standard errors of those for `mid`
and `big` as for `base` (only the intercepts should move, as Section 1 explains). We will see which tools manage that.

## 1. The symptom

Fit the model to the `big` data with the native engine, and compare its standard
errors for the paths and variances with those from the original data:

```{r}
#| label: symptom-medfit
fit_base <- fit_sem(syntax, base, meanstructure = TRUE, information = "expected")
fit_big <- fit_sem(syntax, big, meanstructure = TRUE, information = "expected")
se_base <- sqrt(diag(fit_base@vcov))
se_big <- sqrt(diag(fit_big@vcov))
rd(rbind(base = se_base, big = se_big), 5)
c(largest_difference_in_the_six_path_and_variance_SEs = max(abs(se_big - se_base)[1:6]))
```

```{r}
#| label: symptom-medfit-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(se_big - se_base)[1:6]) < 1e-8, abs(se_big["treatment~1"] - se_base["treatment~1"]) < 1e-8,
          all(se_big[c("mediator1~1", "outcome~1")] > 100 * se_base[c("mediator1~1", "outcome~1")]))
```

The six path and variance standard errors do not move. The last three entries of
each row are the intercepts, and two of their standard errors grow, as they should. An
intercept is the mean of its variable when its *predictors* are at zero, so its standard
error grows with the distance of the predictors' means from zero: the intercept of
`mediator1` is an extrapolation to `treatment` = 0, now 1,000 units from the data, and that
of `outcome` to `mediator1` = `treatment` = 0. The intercept of `treatment` has no
predictors, and its standard error does not move. Now the same model in lavaan and OpenMx:

```{r}
#| label: symptom-others
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)
lav_warn <- NULL
lv <- withCallingHandlers(
  lavaan::sem(syntax, big, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE),
  warning = function(w) {
    lav_warn <<- conditionMessage(w)
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
cat("lavaan warning:", trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ", lav_warn)), "\n\n")

suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
mxOption(NULL, "Number of Threads", 1)
vars <- names(big)
mod <- mxModel("big", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars,
  mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "mediator1", values = 0.4, labels = "a"),
  mxPath(from = c("mediator1", "treatment"), to = "outcome", values = 0.5, labels = c("b", "cp")),
  mxPath(from = vars, arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = paste0("v_", vars)),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = vars, values = colMeans(big), labels = paste0("m_", vars)),
  mxData(big, type = "raw"))
run <- suppressWarnings(mxRun(mod, silent = TRUE))
pt <- summary(run)$parameters
cat("OpenMx optimizer status code:", run$output$status$code, "(0 is success)\n")
paths_mx <- pt[pt$name %in% c("a", "b", "cp"), c("name", "Estimate", "Std.Error")]
paths_mx$ratio_to_native_se <- signif(paths_mx$Std.Error / se_base[paths_mx$name], 2)
paths_mx
```

```{r}
#| label: symptom-others-check
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)
stopifnot(!is.null(lav_warn), min(paths_mx$ratio_to_native_se) > 100)
```

lavaan cannot invert its information matrix and returns no standard errors. OpenMx
reports a nonzero optimizer status and standard errors for the paths that are orders of
magnitude too large: the last column divides each by the native engine's standard error
on the original data, which the first table of this section showed is also the right value for `big`. Neither is a bug in the
estimator's idea; both are the numerical consequence of a nearly singular
information matrix. The next section shows where the singularity comes from.

## 2. Why the information goes singular

The expected information of Chapter 1 has a mean part
$n\,(\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_l\mu)$. It is built from the
derivatives of the implied mean $\mu = F B m$ with $B = (I - A)^{-1}$. Take two
parameters that both move the mean of the same variable $r$: its intercept $m_r$
and one of its paths $A_{r c}$. From Chapter 1, Step 4 of the gradient derivation,

$$
\frac{\partial \mu}{\partial m_r} = F B e_r,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mu}{\partial A_{r c}} = F B e_r \,(B m)_c .
$$

The two derivatives are the same vector, $F B e_r$, and the second is multiplied by
the scalar $(B m)_c$. That scalar is the implied mean of variable $c$,
which at a good fit is close to its sample mean $\bar x_c$. So the mean parts of the
two columns of the information matrix are almost proportional, with a factor of
$\bar x_c$. When $|\bar x_c|$ is large against the standard deviations, the mean part
of the information matrix has two nearly parallel columns, and a matrix with two
nearly parallel columns is nearly singular. Scale the information to unit diagonal,
$I_{kl} / \sqrt{I_{kk} I_{ll}}$: each entry is then the cosine of the angle between two
columns (in the geometry the information defines), and an entry near $\pm 1$ marks a nearly
parallel pair. On the `mid` data:

```{r}
#| label: raw-info
fit_mid <- fit_sem(syntax, mid, meanstructure = TRUE, information = "expected")
ram <- fit_mid@internals$ram
theta <- fit_mid@theta
smp <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fit_mid@data, ram)
info_raw <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(theta, ram, smp, NULL)
# scale to unit diagonal: entry (k, l) is I_kl / sqrt(I_kk I_ll)
cor_raw <- cov2cor(info_raw)
pick <- c("a", "b", "cp", "mediator1~1", "outcome~1")
rd(cor_raw[pick, pick], 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: raw-info-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(cor_raw["a", "mediator1~1"] > 0.9999, cor_raw["b", "outcome~1"] > 0.999)
```

The entry for `a` and `mediator1~1` is `r rd(cor_raw["a", "mediator1~1"], 4)`: that
pair of columns is parallel to four decimals. `b`, `cp` and the intercept of `outcome`
all move the mean of `outcome`, so those three columns are nearly parallel together
(`r rd(cor_raw["b", "outcome~1"], 4)` for `b` and the intercept). The summary the engine
uses to decide whether an information matrix can be inverted is its **Jacobi-scaled
reciprocal condition number**: the reciprocal condition number of the matrix after scaling
it to unit diagonal, so that the units of the parameters play no part. Larger is better,
and the engine treats the matrix as singular below `r format(medfit:::.sem_info_singular_tol)`
(`.sem_info_singular_tol`):

```{r}
#| label: raw-rcond
rcond_scaled <- function(m) rcond(cov2cor(m))
ram_b <- fit_big@internals$ram
smp_b <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fit_big@data, ram_b)
info_raw_b <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(fit_big@theta, ram_b, smp_b, NULL)
c(mid_raw = rcond_scaled(info_raw), big_raw = rcond_scaled(info_raw_b),
  big_raw_unscaled = rcond(info_raw_b), engine_threshold = medfit:::.sem_info_singular_tol)
```

```{r}
#| label: raw-rcond-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(rcond_scaled(info_raw) > medfit:::.sem_info_singular_tol,
          rcond_scaled(info_raw_b) < medfit:::.sem_info_singular_tol, rcond(info_raw_b) < 1e-14)
```

At `mid` scale the raw matrix is poorly conditioned but still above the threshold. At
`big` scale it is below it, and without the Jacobi scaling its reciprocal condition
number is at the level of the machine precision (about $10^{-16}$): the matrix is
singular to working precision, which is what lavaan reported above.

## 3. Centered coordinates

The fix is to describe the same model with different coordinates in which the
paths and the intercepts do not interfere. Let $\bar x_v$ be the sample mean of
variable $v$ (taken as 0 for a latent variable, whose mean is fixed at 0). For
every variable $v$ with a free intercept, define the **centered intercept**

$$
\tilde m_v = m_v - \Bigl(\bar x_v - \sum_c A_{v c}\,\bar x_c\Bigr).
$$

The bracket is the intercept that variable $v$'s equation would need to reproduce
its own sample mean given its paths: if every variable sits at its mean,
$\bar x_v = m_v + \sum_c A_{v c} \bar x_c$, so $m_v = \bar x_v - \sum_c A_{v c}\bar x_c$. (In the
engine the sum runs over the free paths into $v$; Section 5 needs the fixed paths to be zero.)
So $\tilde m_v$ is the amount by which the intercept misses that value, and it
should be near zero at the optimum, whatever the means are, when every intercept is free
(Section 5 shows why). All other parameters
(paths, variances, the intercepts that are not free) keep their own value. Call the
vector of these coordinates $\phi$. Solving the definition for $m_v$ shows $\theta$ is
an affine function of $\phi$,

$$
\theta = T\,(\phi + c_0), \qquad T = I + C, \qquad
C_{k_m(v),\,k_a(v,c)} = -\bar x_c, \qquad (c_0)_{k_m(v)} = \bar x_v ,
$$

where $k_m(v)$ is the position of $v$'s intercept in the parameter vector and
$k_a(v, c)$ that of the path from $c$ to $v$. $C$ has nonzero entries only in the
rows of intercepts and the columns of paths, and $c_0$ only at intercepts. When no intercept
shares a label with a path (condition 3 of Section 5), no intercept position is also a path
position, so $C c_0 = 0$ and $C^2 = 0$. Hence $T^{-1} = I - C$, which gives $\phi = \theta - C\theta - c_0$. The helpers
`.sem_center_map()` and `.sem_to_phi()` build exactly this:

```{r}
#| label: map
ctr <- medfit:::.sem_center_map(ram, smp)
dimnames(ctr$t) <- dimnames(ctr$c) <- list(ram$par_names, ram$par_names)
shifted_rows <- c("mediator1~1", "outcome~1")
cat("The rows of T that differ from the identity (columns: the paths):\n")
rd(ctr$t[shifted_rows, c("a", "b", "cp")], 3)
dev <- ctr$t - diag(ram$q)
dev[shifted_rows, c("a", "b", "cp")] <- 0
cat("\nEvery other entry of T equals the identity: largest deviation =", max(abs(dev)), "\n")
cat("\nc0 (the sample means, at the intercepts)\n")
rd(stats::setNames(ctr$c0, ram$par_names)[c("mediator1~1", "treatment~1", "outcome~1")], 3)
```

Read the two rows: the row `mediator1~1` has $-\bar x_{\text{treatment}}$ in the column
of `a`, since `mediator1`'s only path comes from `treatment`; the row `outcome~1` has
$-\bar x_{\text{mediator1}}$ and $-\bar x_{\text{treatment}}$ in the columns of `b` and `cp`.
Check the algebra, and check that at the fitted
values the centered intercepts are near zero:

```{r}
#| label: map-check
tinv <- diag(ram$q) - ctr$c
phi <- medfit:::.sem_to_phi(theta, ctr)
c(T_times_inverse = max(abs(ctr$t %*% tinv - diag(ram$q))),
  round_trip = max(abs(as.vector(ctr$t %*% (phi + ctr$c0)) - theta)))
rd(stats::setNames(phi, ram$par_names)[c("mediator1~1", "treatment~1", "outcome~1")], 8)
```

```{r}
#| label: map-check-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(ctr$t %*% tinv - diag(ram$q))) < 1e-12,
          max(abs(phi[ram$par_names %in% c("mediator1~1", "treatment~1", "outcome~1")])) < 1e-6)
```

The intercepts of `mediator1` and `outcome` in $\phi$ are zero to 8 decimals (the
`treatment` intercept has no path entering it, so $\tilde m$ equals $m - \bar x$ and
it is zero because the free mean of an exogenous variable is its sample mean).
This is no accident, and Section 5 explains it.

## 4. Information and covariance in the new coordinates

Because $\theta = T(\phi + c_0)$ is affine, the gradient and Hessian of the
discrepancy follow by the chain rule. For $F(\phi) = F_{ML}(T(\phi + c_0))$,
$\nabla_\phi F = T^\top \nabla_\theta F$ and $\nabla^2_\phi F = T^\top (\nabla^2_\theta F)\,T$ (there is no term
from the second derivative of the map, because it is affine). So the information in the
new coordinates is $I_\phi = T^\top I_\theta T$, and the covariance of the estimates
transforms in the opposite direction:

$$
I_\phi = T^\top I_\theta\, T
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
V_\theta = I_\theta^{-1} = T\, I_\phi^{-1}\, T^\top = T\, V_\phi\, T^\top .
$$

The engine builds $I_\phi$ (`.sem_info_expected(..., ctr)` for the expected
information; the observed one takes the Hessian directly in $\phi$, along the
columns of $T$), inverts it, and maps back. The mean part of $I_\phi$ uses
$\partial\mu/\partial\phi$, the derivative of Section 2 with the path columns changed
to $F B e_r\,[(B m)_c - \bar x_c]$. The bracket is the gap between the implied and the sample
mean of $c$, which is close to zero at the fit, so the two nearly parallel columns of
Section 2 have been pulled apart. See the conditioning, and check the identity on the
`mid` data, where the raw matrix can still be inverted:

```{r}
#| label: info-phi
info_phi <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(theta, ram, smp, ctr)
c(raw = rcond_scaled(info_raw), centered = rcond_scaled(info_phi))
v_phi <- solve(info_phi)
v_back <- ctr$t %*% v_phi %*% t(ctr$t)
c(
  chain_rule = max(abs(info_phi - t(ctr$t) %*% info_raw %*% ctr$t)) / max(abs(info_phi)),
  V_equals_T_Vphi_Tt = max(abs(v_back - solve(info_raw))) / max(abs(v_back)),
  engine_vcov = max(abs(v_back - fit_mid@vcov)) / max(abs(v_back))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: info-phi-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(rcond_scaled(info_phi) > 0.1,
          max(abs(info_phi - t(ctr$t) %*% info_raw %*% ctr$t)) / max(abs(info_phi)) < 1e-8,
          max(abs(v_back - solve(info_raw))) / max(abs(v_back)) < 1e-6,
          max(abs(v_back - fit_mid@vcov)) / max(abs(v_back)) < 1e-10)
```

The centered information is well conditioned, the chain rule holds to rounding, and
the covariance the engine reports equals $T V_\phi T^\top$. At `big` scale there is no
raw inverse to compare with, but the centered route still works. Its path and variance
standard errors were already shown in Section 1 to equal those of the original data, and
its conditioning is:

```{r}
#| label: info-phi-big
ctr_b <- medfit:::.sem_center_map(ram_b, smp_b)
c(raw = rcond_scaled(info_raw_b),
  centered = rcond_scaled(medfit:::.sem_info_expected(fit_big@theta, ram_b, smp_b, ctr_b)))
```

### The same comparison against lavaan and OpenMx

On the `mid` data every package can invert its information. We compare the nine
standard errors with lavaan's from the same information (expected, then observed) and with
OpenMx's, which come from a numerical Hessian and so correspond to the observed information:

```{r}
#| label: se-compare
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)
f_exp <- fit_sem(syntax, mid, meanstructure = TRUE, information = "expected")
f_obs <- fit_sem(syntax, mid, meanstructure = TRUE, information = "observed")
lv_exp <- lavaan::sem(syntax, mid, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE, information = "expected")
lv_obs <- lavaan::sem(syntax, mid, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE, information = "observed")

vars <- names(mid)
mod_mid <- mxModel("mid", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars,
  mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "mediator1", values = 0.4, labels = "a"),
  mxPath(from = c("mediator1", "treatment"), to = "outcome", values = 0.5, labels = c("b", "cp")),
  mxPath(from = vars, arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = paste0("v_", vars)),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = vars, values = colMeans(mid), labels = paste0("m_", vars)),
  mxData(mid, type = "raw"))
run_mid <- mxRun(mod_mid, silent = TRUE)
pt_mid <- summary(run_mid)$parameters
se_mx <- stats::setNames(pt_mid$Std.Error, pt_mid$name)
mx_name <- c(a = "a", b = "b", cp = "cp", "mediator1~~mediator1" = "v_mediator1",
             "outcome~~outcome" = "v_outcome", "treatment~~treatment" = "v_treatment",
             "mediator1~1" = "m_mediator1", "treatment~1" = "m_treatment", "outcome~1" = "m_outcome")
nm <- names(mx_name)
rel <- function(x, y) max(abs(x - y) / y)
c(
  `expected: medfit vs lavaan` = rel(sqrt(diag(f_exp@vcov))[nm], sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_exp)))[nm]),
  `observed: medfit vs lavaan` = rel(sqrt(diag(f_obs@vcov))[nm], sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_obs)))[nm]),
  `observed: medfit vs OpenMx` = rel(sqrt(diag(f_obs@vcov))[nm], se_mx[mx_name])
)
```

```{r}
#| label: se-compare-check
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)
stopifnot(rel(sqrt(diag(f_exp@vcov))[nm], sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_exp)))[nm]) < 1e-6,
          rel(sqrt(diag(f_obs@vcov))[nm], sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_obs)))[nm]) < 1e-6,
          rel(sqrt(diag(f_obs@vcov))[nm], se_mx[mx_name]) < 1e-3)
```

Each entry is the largest relative difference over the nine standard errors.

## 5. The shifted-data fit, and why it is exact

The centered coordinates fix the information. The engine goes one step further when it
can: it fits the model to data from which the sample means have been subtracted, and
maps the solution back. Why is that allowed? Here is the argument, in three steps.

**Step 1: profile out the intercepts.** Suppose every observed variable has its own free,
unconstrained intercept. For any fixed paths $A$ and variances $S_{\text{ram}}$, choose
$m = (I - A)\bar x$ (with $\bar x$ padded with zeros for latent variables, which this
argument excludes below). Then $\mu = F B m = F B (I - A) \bar x = F\bar x = \bar x$. The
gap $d = \bar x - \mu$ of Chapter 1 is zero, so the mean term vanishes, which is its
smallest possible value. So for each $(A, S_{\text{ram}})$ the best intercepts are those, and the
discrepancy that remains,

$$
\min_m F_{ML}(A, S_{\text{ram}}, m) = \log|\Sigma| + \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) - \log|S| - p,
$$

involves the data only through $S$, the sample covariance.

**Step 2: $S$ does not change under a shift.** Subtracting $\bar x$ from every row changes
the means and leaves the covariance matrix alone. So the profile function, and therefore the
minimizing $(A, S_{\text{ram}})$, are the same for the original and the centered data.

**Step 3: map the intercepts back.** On the centered data the sample mean is 0, and the
intercepts that solve Step 1 are $\tilde m = (I - A) \cdot 0 = 0$: the centered fit has
$\tilde m = 0$ at the optimum, as Section 3 saw. On the original data they are
$m = (I - A)\bar x$, which is $\theta = T(\phi + c_0)$ with $\phi$ the centered solution
(for variable $v$, $m_v = \tilde m_v + \bar x_v - \sum_c A_{v c}\bar x_c$).

This also explains the $\phi$ values in Section 3 and gives something to check: the
mean-structure fit has no mean discrepancy left, and its paths and variances equal those
of the covariance-only fit.

```{r}
#| label: profile
# a model with one restriction (df = 1), so the discrepancy is not zero
restricted <- paste0(syntax, "cp == 0\n")
fit_cov <- fit_sem(restricted, big)                              # no intercepts: covariance only
fit_ms <- fit_sem(restricted, big, meanstructure = TRUE)         # with free intercepts
ram_r <- fit_ms@internals$ram
gap <- colMeans(fit_ms@data) - medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram_r, fit_ms@theta)
common <- names(fit_cov@theta)
c(F_covariance_only = fit_cov@f, F_with_means = fit_ms@f,
  largest_difference_in_shared_estimates = max(abs(fit_ms@theta[common] - fit_cov@theta)),
  mean_gap_xbar_minus_mu = max(abs(gap)))
```

```{r}
#| label: profile-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(fit_cov@f > 0, abs(fit_cov@f - fit_ms@f) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(fit_ms@theta[common] - fit_cov@theta)) < 1e-8, max(abs(gap)) < 1e-6)
```

The two discrepancies are the same nonzero number, the shared estimates agree, and the mean gap
$\bar x - \mu$ is zero (to the tolerance of the optimizer), on data whose means are 1,000 to
100,000 units from zero.

Now the shifted fit itself, on the unrestricted model. Fit the centered data, map the solution back with
$T(\phi + c_0)$, and compare with `fit_big`:

```{r}
#| label: shifted
centered <- as.data.frame(scale(big, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE))
fit_c <- fit_sem(syntax, centered, meanstructure = TRUE)
c0_b <- ctr_b$c0
back <- as.vector(ctr_b$t %*% (fit_c@theta + c0_b))
cat("centered-data intercepts (phi):\n")
rd(fit_c@theta[c("mediator1~1", "treatment~1", "outcome~1")], 10)
c(largest_difference_after_mapping_back = max(abs(back - fit_big@theta)))
```

```{r}
#| label: shifted-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(back - fit_big@theta)) < 1e-8,
          max(abs(fit_c@theta[c("mediator1~1", "treatment~1", "outcome~1")])) < 1e-8)
```

The intercepts on the centered data are zero, and the mapped-back solution equals `fit_big`.
That comparison only shows that we reproduced the engine's route, since `fit_big` itself came
out of the shifted path. The independent check is the refused-shift comparison below, which fits
the same data without the shift.

### When the shift is allowed

Step 1 needs every intercept to be free to take the value $(I - A)\bar x$, and the
back-map of Step 3 needs the paths to carry the shift through $T$. `.sem_shift_ok()` in
`R/sem-fit.R` checks, in this order:

1. the model has a mean structure, and some free intercept belongs to a variable that
   has a free path entering it (otherwise there is no map to undo);
2. every free intercept is its own parameter (no shared label), none has a user start
   value, and none has a bound;
3. every observed variable has a free intercept or, under `fixed_x` (Chapter 4), a mean
   held at its sample value, and no intercept shares a label with a path;
4. there is no fixed nonzero path, and every free path enters an observed variable
   (a path into a latent variable cannot absorb the shift, because the latent mean is fixed at 0;
   a latent variable's marker loading is also a fixed nonzero path);
5. no intercept appears in a constraint.

Constraints on paths and variances are allowed, because the argument never touches
them. We test the rule by building each situation and asking the function, replicating
the first steps of `fit_sem()` to get its arguments:

```{r}
#| label: shift-ok
shift_ok <- function(text, data, meanstructure = TRUE) {
  parsed <- medfit:::.sem_parse(text)
  tab <- medfit:::.sem_complete(parsed$parameters, meanstructure)
  conv <- medfit:::.sem_to_ram(tab)
  r <- conv$ram
  s <- medfit:::.sem_sample(data[, r$obs], r)
  given <- !is.na(conv$start)
  lb <- ifelse(is.na(conv$lower), -Inf, conv$lower)
  ub <- ifelse(is.na(conv$upper), Inf, conv$upper)
  medfit:::.sem_shift_ok(r, s, parsed$constraints, lb, ub, given)
}
cases <- c(
  "all intercepts free" = syntax,
  "constraint on paths (a == b)" = paste0(syntax, "\na == b"),
  "outcome ~ 0*1 (a fixed intercept)" = paste0(syntax, "\noutcome ~ 0*1"),
  "an intercept in a constraint" = paste0(syntax, "\nmediator1 ~ k*1\nk == 5"),
  "a start value on an intercept" = paste0(syntax, "\nmediator1 ~ start(5)*1"),
  "a bound on an intercept" = paste0(syntax, "\nmediator1 ~ lower(0)*1"),
  "one label on two intercepts" = paste0(syntax, "\nmediator1 ~ k*1\noutcome ~ k*1"),
  "an intercept sharing a path's label" = paste0(syntax, "\nmediator1 ~ a*1"),
  "a fixed nonzero path" = "mediator1 ~ a * treatment\noutcome ~ b * mediator1 + 0.5 * treatment",
  "a latent variable (and a path into it)" = "M =~ mediator1 + outcome\nM ~ treatment"
)
allowed <- vapply(cases, shift_ok, NA, data = mid)
data.frame(model = names(cases), shift_allowed = allowed, row.names = NULL)
shift_ok(syntax, mid, meanstructure = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: shift-ok-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(identical(unname(allowed), c(TRUE, TRUE, rep(FALSE, 8))), !shift_ok(syntax, mid, meanstructure = FALSE))
```

The last line is the model without a mean structure (condition 1): there are no
intercepts to profile, and the answer is `FALSE`.

### What happens when the shift is refused

A refusal does not mean failure. The engine then optimizes in the original
coordinates, with the same **acceptance gate** (the engine's test, applied to every solution,
that the solver really stopped at a minimum; Chapter 3 derives it, and it still uses the centered
Hessian when a mean structure is present) and, for a model without constraints, a Newton polish in the
centered coordinates after the solver stops (`.sem_polish_centered()`, which takes a few
Newton steps on the centered Hessian). To see it, give the
`mediator1` intercept a start value (an innocuous request that condition 2 refuses) and
compare with the shifted fit, on both data sets:

```{r}
#| label: refused
compare_refused <- function(d) {
  fast <- fit_sem(syntax, d, meanstructure = TRUE)
  start_txt <- paste0(syntax, "\nmediator1 ~ start(", round(mean(d$mediator1) * 0.95), ")*1")
  slow <- fit_sem(start_txt, d)
  data.frame(shift_allowed_default = shift_ok(syntax, d), shift_allowed_with_start = shift_ok(start_txt, d),
             largest_estimate_difference = max(abs(fast@theta - slow@theta[names(fast@theta)])))
}
refused <- rbind(mid = compare_refused(mid), big = compare_refused(big))
refused
```

```{r}
#| label: refused-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(all(refused$shift_allowed_default), !any(refused$shift_allowed_with_start),
          all(refused$largest_estimate_difference < 1e-6))
```

The two routes return the same estimates, so the shift is an optimization and not a
requirement. What it buys is a better-behaved problem for the solver. To see that, run
SLSQP (the solver, Chapter 3) once on each version of the data from the engine's default
start, and judge each solution with the engine's acceptance gate. The gate builds the
curvature in centered coordinates in both cases, so it can judge the raw-coordinate solution
fairly:

```{r}
#| label: iterations
opts <- list(algorithm = "NLOPT_LD_SLSQP", xtol_rel = 1e-10, ftol_rel = 1e-12, maxeval = 10000L)
solve_once <- function(d, centered) {
  f <- fit_sem(syntax, d, meanstructure = TRUE)
  r0 <- f@internals$ram
  dd <- if (centered) as.data.frame(scale(d, scale = FALSE)) else d
  sm <- medfit:::.sem_sample(dd, r0)
  lb <- rep(-Inf, r0$q)
  ub <- rep(Inf, r0$q)
  res <- medfit:::.sem_solve_one(medfit:::.sem_default_start(r0, sm), r0, sm, lb, ub, opts)
  gate <- medfit:::.sem_gate(res$solution, res$status, r0, sm, lb, ub)
  data.frame(nlopt_status = res$status, iterations = res$iterations, accepted = gate$accepted,
             newton_decrement = signif(gate$decrement, 2))
}
runs <- rbind(mid_original = solve_once(mid, FALSE), mid_centered = solve_once(mid, TRUE),
              big_original = solve_once(big, FALSE), big_centered = solve_once(big, TRUE))
runs
```

```{r}
#| label: iterations-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(all(runs$accepted), all(runs$newton_decrement < 1e-3),
          runs["mid_centered", "iterations"] < runs["mid_original", "iterations"],
          runs["big_centered", "iterations"] < runs["big_original", "iterations"])
```

All four runs are accepted. The Newton decrement is the gate's measure of how far the solution is
from a stationary point (the gradient measured in the units of the curvature; Chapter 3 defines it),
and it is far below the gate's threshold of $10^{-3}$ in every run. The status column gives the reason
the solver stopped (3: the objective stopped changing; 4: the parameters stopped moving). The centered
data need fewer iterations at both scales, although the engine already rescales every parameter by its
natural unit before calling the solver (Chapter 3), which removes much of the difference in units.

## Check yourself

1. Add 50 to every value of `outcome`. Which of the following change: the path $b$,
   the variance of `outcome`, the intercept of `outcome`, the standard error of $b$?
   (Answer: only the intercept; the chunk after this list runs it.)
2. Why does condition 3 say "every observed variable"? (Answer: Step 1 sets
   $\mu = \bar x$ for all observed variables at once; one fixed intercept leaves a
   mean gap that depends on the location of the data.)
3. Why is $C^2 = 0$? (Answer: $C$ has nonzero columns only at path parameters
   and nonzero rows only at intercept parameters, and when no intercept shares a label with a
   path, which the shift requires, no position is both.)

```{r}
#| label: shift-outcome
moved <- fit_sem(syntax, transform(base, outcome = outcome + 50), meanstructure = TRUE)
orig <- fit_sem(syntax, base, meanstructure = TRUE)
rd(moved@theta - orig@theta, 6)
rd(sqrt(diag(moved@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(orig@vcov)), 6)
```

```{r}
#| label: shift-outcome-check
#| include: false
dth <- moved@theta - orig@theta
stopifnot(abs(dth["outcome~1"] - 50) < 1e-6, max(abs(dth[names(dth) != "outcome~1"])) < 1e-6,
          max(abs(sqrt(diag(moved@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(orig@vcov)))) < 1e-6)
```

The first line is the change in each estimate and the second the change in each standard
error, after adding 50 to `outcome`: the intercept of `outcome` moves by 50 and nothing else
does, not even a standard error. (The standard error of an intercept depends on where the
*predictors* sit, as Section 1 showed by shifting them; this shift leaves them alone.)
